prompt: In the rule p { color: blue; }, which part is the selector?
optionB: p
optionC: blue
optionD: color: blue
correctAnswerText: p
explanation: The selector says which elements the rule applies to and sits before the braces. What follows inside is a property and its value.

prompt: In the same rule, which part is the property?
optionB: blue
optionC: color: blue
optionD: color
correctAnswerText: color
explanation: The property names what is being set and the value says what it is set to. The two together make one declaration.

prompt: In the rule .btn { font-size: 14px; }, which part is the value?
optionB: .btn
optionC: font-size
optionD: font-size: 14px
correctAnswerText: 14px
explanation: The value 14px follows the colon and says what the property is being set to. Naming the whole declaration answers a different question.

prompt: How many declarations does the rule h1 { color: red; font-size: 20px; } contain?
optionB: Three
optionC: Two
optionD: Four
correctAnswerText: Two
explanation: Each property-and-value pair is one declaration, and there are two inside the braces. The selector is not a declaration.

prompt: A rule reads .note { margin: 10px; padding: 5px; }. How many elements does it configure, and how many things does it set on each?
optionA: One element, and two things on it
optionB: Every element carrying that class, and two things on each
optionC: Every element carrying that class, and one thing on each
optionD: Two elements, one per declaration
correctAnswerText: Every element carrying that class, and two things on each
explanation: A selector matches a set of elements, however many there are, and every declaration inside applies to each of them. The number of declarations has nothing to do with the number of elements.

prompt: Space is wanted between an element's border and its content. Which property produces it?
optionB: border
optionC: width
optionD: padding
correctAnswerText: padding
explanation: The space inside the border, between it and the content, is padding. Margin sits outside the border and pushes other elements away instead.

prompt: Space is wanted between an element and the one beside it. Which property produces it?
optionB: padding
optionC: border
optionD: height
correctAnswerText: margin
explanation: Margin is space outside the element, which is what separates it from its neighbours. Padding would make the element itself larger and move nothing else away.

prompt: The text of a paragraph should be green. Which property sets it?
optionB: border-color
optionC: color
optionD: font-size
correctAnswerText: color
explanation: The colour property sets the colour of the text itself. The background property fills the area behind it, which is the pair most often mixed up.

prompt: A developer adds padding expecting the element to move away from its neighbour, and the neighbour does not move. Why?
optionA: Padding only works on text elements
optionB: Padding grows the element inwards from its edge; moving neighbours away is what margin does
optionC: Padding was applied to the wrong side
optionD: The neighbour has a margin cancelling it
correctAnswerText: Padding grows the element inwards from its edge; moving neighbours away is what margin does
explanation: The element does get larger, so something visibly changed and the neighbour still touches its edge. Which side the padding was applied to would change where the space appeared and not whether the neighbour moved.

prompt: What does the selector .warning target?
optionA: The one element whose identifier is warning
optionB: Every element named warning
optionC: The first element carrying the class warning
optionD: Every element carrying the class warning
correctAnswerText: Every element carrying the class warning
explanation: A leading dot marks a class, which any number of elements may carry. An identifier is marked differently and is meant to appear once.

prompt: What does the selector #total target?
optionA: The element whose identifier is total
optionB: Every element carrying the class total
optionC: Every element named total
optionD: Every element containing the word total
correctAnswerText: The element whose identifier is total
explanation: A leading hash marks an identifier, which is meant to be unique within the page. Swapping the two prefixes is the commonest selector mistake.

prompt: What does the selector nav a target?
optionA: Every navigation element and every link
optionB: Every navigation element that is also a link
optionC: Every link inside a navigation element
optionD: The first link inside a navigation element
correctAnswerText: Every link inside a navigation element
explanation: A space between two selectors means "inside", so the second is looked for within the first. Reading it as two separate selectors would target both kinds of element.

prompt: How does the selector p.note differ from p .note, with a space?
optionA: They are the same; the space is ignored
optionB: The first targets paragraphs carrying the class; the second targets elements with the class inside a paragraph
optionC: The first targets any element with the class inside a paragraph
optionD: The second targets paragraphs carrying the class
correctAnswerText: The first targets paragraphs carrying the class; the second targets elements with the class inside a paragraph
explanation: Without a space the two conditions apply to one element; with a space the second is looked for inside the first. The space is the whole difference and is easy to add or lose by accident.

prompt:
Markup:

A

B

C

. How many elements does .note match?
optionB: Three
optionC: None
optionD: Two
correctAnswerText: Two
explanation: A class selector matches every element carrying the class wherever it appears, so both marked paragraphs match. Assuming a class matches one element confuses it with an identifier.

prompt:
A menu is written as
  • Home
  • About
. Which selector reaches the About entry and nothing else?
optionB: .item
optionC: #menu li
optionD: li
correctAnswerText: .current
explanation: Only the second entry carries current, so .current isolates it. The other three each reach both entries, because both carry item and both sit inside the menu.

prompt: A colour is set on a container. Do the paragraphs inside it take that colour?
optionA: No; every property must be set on each element
optionB: Only if the paragraphs have no colour of their own and no class
optionC: Yes; colour is one of the properties children inherit
optionD: Only the first paragraph does
correctAnswerText: Yes; colour is one of the properties children inherit
explanation: Text-related properties pass down to children unless something overrides them. A paragraph with its own colour would use that instead, which is different from needing one.

prompt: A border is set on a container. Do the paragraphs inside it get a border?
optionA: Yes; children inherit everything from a parent
optionB: No; a border is not inherited
optionC: Yes; borders inherit in the same way as colour
optionD: Only the paragraphs with no border of their own
correctAnswerText: No; a border is not inherited
explanation: Some properties inherit and others do not, and box properties such as borders are in the second group. Assuming inheritance is all-or-nothing gets one of the two cases wrong whichever way it is assumed.

prompt: Two rules both target the same paragraph with equal specificity: the first sets the colour to red and the second to blue. Which applies?
optionA: Red, because the first rule was applied first
optionB: Neither; the conflict cancels both
optionC: Both, blended together
optionD: Blue, because the later rule wins when specificity is equal
correctAnswerText: Blue, because the later rule wins when specificity is equal
explanation: Order decides only when specificity is level, which it is here. Nothing blends or cancels — one value is used.

prompt: A rule .note { color: red; } appears first, and p { color: blue; } appears after it. A paragraph carries the class note. Which colour applies?
optionA: Red, because the class selector is more specific than the element selector
optionB: Blue, because it appears later
optionC: Blue, because element selectors are stronger
optionD: Neither; the two cancel out
correctAnswerText: Red, because the class selector is more specific than the element selector
explanation: Specificity is considered before order, so a later rule loses to a more specific earlier one. This is the case where "the last rule wins" gives the wrong answer.

prompt: A developer moves a rule to the bottom of the stylesheet to make it win, and the colour does not change. Their rule uses an element selector and the competing rule uses a class. What happened?
optionB: The move introduced a syntax error
optionC: The competing rule is more specific, and moving a rule later does not overcome that
optionD: The rule is now too late in the file to apply
correctAnswerText: The competing rule is more specific, and moving a rule later does not overcome that
explanation: Order is only consulted when specificity ties, so a more specific rule wins from anywhere in the file. The move was based on a rule that holds only in the equal-specificity case.

prompt: Which is more specific: p or .note?
optionB: .note
optionC: They are equal
optionD: It depends which appears first
correctAnswerText: .note
explanation: A class outranks an element selector regardless of order. Order is only consulted when the two are level.

prompt: Which is more specific: body div section p, or .note?
optionA: body div section p, since it has four parts
optionB: They are equal
optionC: It depends which appears first
optionD: .note
correctAnswerText: .note
explanation: Specificity compares the kinds of selector rather than how many there are, and one class outranks any number of element selectors. Length is the intuition this case exists to break.

prompt: A developer adds three more element names to their selector to make it beat a class rule, and it still loses. Their selector is now six elements long. Why?
optionA: Element selectors never accumulate into a class's worth of specificity, however many are added
optionB: Six is too many selectors to combine
optionC: The class rule appears later in the file
optionD: The extra elements do not match the markup
correctAnswerText: Element selectors never accumulate into a class's worth of specificity, however many are added
explanation: The comparison is made level by level, and no quantity of the weaker kind reaches the stronger. Adding more of what is already losing cannot change the outcome.

prompt: An element has a content width of 100px and padding of 10px on each side, with no border. How wide is it in total?
optionB: 110px
optionC: 120px
optionD: 140px
correctAnswerText: 120px
explanation: Padding is added on both sides, so twice ten is added to the content width. Counting one side only gives 110.

prompt: An element must end up occupying exactly 240px across. It carries padding of 15px on each side and a border of 5px on each side. What content width is needed?
optionB: 200px
optionC: 220px
optionD: 210px
correctAnswerText: 200px
explanation: Padding and border are both doubled, so forty of the 240 is taken before the content, leaving 200px. Subtracting only one side of each leaves 220.

prompt: An element has a content width of 100px, padding of 10px each side and a margin of 20px each side. A developer says it occupies 160px. The question asks for the width of the element itself, not the space it reserves. What is it?
optionB: 100px, since padding is inside the content
optionC: 140px, counting the margin on one side
optionD: 120px; the margin is outside the element rather than part of it
correctAnswerText: 120px; the margin is outside the element rather than part of it
explanation: Margin is space around the element and belongs to no element's own width. The 160 answers a different and reasonable question — how much horizontal space is reserved — which is why the stem says which is being asked.

prompt: Two block elements follow one another in the markup. How are they arranged?
optionB: Side by side
optionC: Overlapping
optionD: Side by side if there is room
correctAnswerText: Stacked, one below the other
explanation: A block element takes the full width available, so the next one starts on a new line. Sitting side by side is what inline elements do.

prompt: Two inline elements follow one another in the markup. How are they arranged?
optionB: Side by side, never wrapping
optionC: Side by side, wrapping to the next line if there is not room
optionD: Overlapping
correctAnswerText: Side by side, wrapping to the next line if there is not room
explanation: Inline elements flow like words in a sentence and wrap when the line runs out. That flow is exactly what distinguishes them from block elements.

prompt: A developer sets a width on an inline element and nothing changes. The rule is being applied and the selector matches. Why is the width ignored?
optionB: An inline element is sized by its content, so a width has no effect on it
optionC: A more specific rule is setting the width
optionD: The element has no content to size
correctAnswerText: An inline element is sized by its content, so a width has no effect on it
explanation: The stem rules out the rule not applying, so the value is reaching the element and doing nothing. Width applies to elements that participate in block layout, which an inline element does not.

prompt: A child element is given a width of 50%. What is that a percentage of?
optionB: The width of the whole page
optionC: Its own content width
optionD: Its parent's width
correctAnswerText: Its parent's width
explanation: A percentage width resolves against the containing element. Resolving it against the screen would give the same answer only when the parent happens to fill the screen.

prompt: A container has a font size of 20px and a child is given a font size of 1.5 of the inherited size. What size is the child's text?
optionB: 1.5px
optionC: 24px, based on a 16px default
optionD: 20px
correctAnswerText: 30px
explanation: A relative font unit multiplies the size inherited from the parent, which is 20 here. Resolving it against the document default ignores the inheritance.

prompt: A developer sets a font size in pixels and a reader's enlarged text setting has no effect on it. The setting works on the rest of the page. What accounts for it?
optionB: The rule is more specific than the reader's setting
optionC: A fixed unit does not scale with the reader's preference, while relative units do
optionD: Pixels are a relative unit and should have scaled
correctAnswerText: A fixed unit does not scale with the reader's preference, while relative units do
explanation: Fixed units mean exactly what they say and ignore the reader's preference, which is the whole difference from relative ones. The rest of the page scaling shows the setting itself is working.

prompt: Three block elements sit inside a container whose display is set to arrange its children in a row. How are they arranged?
optionA: Stacked one below the other, as blocks normally are
optionB: Side by side in a row
optionC: Overlapping at the same position
optionD: Side by side only if each is given a width
correctAnswerText: Side by side in a row
explanation: The container's arrangement governs how its children are laid out, overriding their default block behaviour. Nothing further is needed to place them in a row.

prompt: A container arranges its children in a row, and one child also has a rule stacking its own children below one another. Both rules are valid and both apply. What is the result?
optionB: Everything sits in a row
optionC: The two rules conflict and neither applies
optionD: The children of the container sit in a row, and inside one of them its own children are stacked
correctAnswerText: The children of the container sit in a row, and inside one of them its own children are stacked
explanation: Each container governs only its own children, so the two rules act at different levels and both take effect. Reading them as competing assumes one arrangement applies to the whole page.

prompt: A stylesheet has base rules and a conditional block applying at widths of 600px and above. The screen is 800px wide. Which styles are in effect?
optionA: Both; the conditional block adds to the base rules rather than replacing them
optionB: Only the conditional block
optionC: Only the base rules
optionD: Neither, since the conditions overlap
correctAnswerText: Both; the conditional block adds to the base rules rather than replacing them
explanation: Conditional rules are ordinary rules that apply when their condition holds, so they join the cascade rather than replacing what came before. Anything they do not mention keeps its base value.

prompt: A conditional block applies at widths of 600px and above. The screen is exactly 600px. Does it apply?
optionB: It is undefined at exactly the boundary
optionC: Yes; "and above" includes the boundary value itself
optionD: Only if another condition also holds
correctAnswerText: Yes; "and above" includes the boundary value itself
explanation: The condition includes its endpoint, so the boundary width is covered. This is the same boundary reasoning as any inclusive comparison, and it is where two adjacent conditional blocks can overlap or leave a gap.

prompt: A rule targeting .btn has no effect, and the developer tools show the rule is not listed against the element at all. What is the cause?
optionA: A more specific rule is overriding it
optionB: The selector does not match the element
optionC: The stylesheet is cached
optionD: The property is misspelled
correctAnswerText: The selector does not match the element
explanation: A rule that loses the cascade is still listed against the element, struck through. Not being listed at all means the selector never matched.

prompt: A rule has no effect. The developer tools list it against the element with its value struck through. The selector clearly matches and the file is loading. What is the cause?
optionB: The stylesheet failed to load
optionC: The property name is misspelled
optionD: Another rule won the cascade for that property
correctAnswerText: Another rule won the cascade for that property
explanation: Being listed means the selector matched and the file loaded; being struck through means it lost to something else. A misspelled property would be listed as unrecognised rather than overridden.

prompt: Three causes make a style fail to appear: the selector does not match, the rule lost the cascade, or the file did not load. Which single piece of evidence separates them fastest?
optionA: The developer tools' list of rules for that element: absent, struck through, or the whole file missing
optionB: Reloading the page
optionC: Reading the stylesheet again
optionD: Adding the style directly to the element
correctAnswerText: The developer tools' list of rules for that element: absent, struck through, or the whole file missing
explanation: The rules panel distinguishes all three at once, because each cause leaves a different trace. Applying the style directly proves it can work and says nothing about which cause was blocking it.

prompt: A developer fixes a style that would not apply by marking it as most important. It now works. What has that established about the original cause?
optionB: That the file was not loading
optionC: Only that the rule can win when forced; it does not say why it was losing, or whether it matched before
optionD: That another rule was overriding it
correctAnswerText: Only that the rule can win when forced; it does not say why it was losing, or whether it matched before
explanation: Forcing a rule to win changes the outcome without revealing the cause, and it would not have worked had the selector never matched — so it does narrow things slightly. What it mainly does is close the investigation before the cause is known.

prompt: A style applies on the developer's machine and not for other users. The stylesheet on the server contains the rule. What is the likely cause?
optionA: The selector does not match for other users
optionB: Other users are being served a stored copy of the stylesheet from before the rule was added
optionC: The rule is invalid for other browsers
optionD: The developer's browser is applying an extra rule
correctAnswerText: Other users are being served a stored copy of the stylesheet from before the rule was added
explanation: A split between the developer and everyone else, with the server holding the right file, is what a stored copy produces. The selector and the markup are the same for everybody.

prompt: A style from a library cannot be edited and must be overridden on one component. Every option below would win. Which has the least collateral effect?
optionA: A rule marked as most important, applied to the element type
optionB: A rule targeting the element type across the whole page
optionC: An inline style on every instance of the component
optionD: A rule with a slightly higher specificity, targeting only that component
correctAnswerText: A rule with a slightly higher specificity, targeting only that component
explanation: Winning is not the difficulty; every option does that. What separates them is how much else they touch and how hard they make the next override — marking a rule most important wins and leaves nothing above it.

prompt: An override relies on appearing later in the file than the rule it beats. What is the risk?
optionA: If the load order changes, the override silently stops working
optionB: There is no risk; order is fixed
optionC: The override will apply twice
optionD: The override will affect other elements
correctAnswerText: If the load order changes, the override silently stops working
explanation: Order-based wins depend on something outside the rule itself, and load order is not always under the author's control. An override that wins on specificity does not care when it is loaded.

prompt: Marking a rule as most important wins reliably. Why is it a poor first choice?
optionB: It is slower to apply
optionC: It leaves nothing stronger for the next override, so the next problem has no clean solution
optionD: It only works on some properties
correctAnswerText: It leaves nothing stronger for the next override, so the next problem has no clean solution
explanation: It works, which is why it is reached for. The cost is paid later, when somebody needs to override the override and the ordinary tools have already been exhausted.

prompt: An override is written with a very long, highly specific selector so that it certainly wins. What does that cost?
optionB: It ties the rule to the current markup, so it stops applying if the structure changes
optionC: It slows the page noticeably
optionD: It affects elements elsewhere on the page
correctAnswerText: It ties the rule to the current markup, so it stops applying if the structure changes
explanation: A long selector describes a path through the document, and every element in it becomes something the rule depends on. Rearranging the markup then breaks styling that has nothing wrong with it.

prompt: What is the general principle behind choosing an override?
optionA: Always win by the largest margin available
optionB: Always rely on order, which is simplest
optionC: Avoid overriding library styles at all
optionD: Win by the smallest margin that is robust, so later changes still have room to work
correctAnswerText: Win by the smallest margin that is robust, so later changes still have room to work
explanation: Every override is followed by another one eventually, and the choice made now decides what is available then. Winning by as much as possible and refusing to override at all are both ways of avoiding the judgement.

prompt: Two rule sets produce an identical page for the markup shown: one targets .note and one targets p. The markup contains exactly one paragraph, which carries the class note. Are they equivalent?
optionA: No; they differ as soon as a paragraph without the class, or a non-paragraph with it, is added
optionB: Yes; the page is identical
optionC: No; they differ in appearance already
optionD: Yes, provided the markup is not changed
correctAnswerText: No; they differ as soon as a paragraph without the class, or a non-paragraph with it, is added
explanation: The two selectors happen to select the same single element here and describe different sets. Equivalence for one document is much weaker than equivalence for the documents it might become.

prompt: Two rules set the same property to the same value and differ only in specificity. Nothing else currently competes for that property. Are they equivalent?
optionB: No; different specificity always changes the result
optionC: For now yes, and they will differ as soon as another rule competes for the property
optionD: No; the more specific rule renders differently
correctAnswerText: For now yes, and they will differ as soon as another rule competes for the property
explanation: Specificity has no effect until there is a competition, so today the two are indistinguishable. What differs is how each behaves when the stylesheet grows.

prompt: Two stylesheets differ only in the order of two rules that target different, non-overlapping sets of elements. Are they equivalent?
optionA: No; order always matters in a stylesheet
optionB: Yes; order matters only between rules competing for the same property on the same element
optionC: No; the later rule always wins
optionD: Yes, but only if both use the same selector kind
correctAnswerText: Yes; order matters only between rules competing for the same property on the same element
explanation: Two rules that never apply to the same element cannot compete, so their relative order is invisible. Order is a tie-breaker rather than a general property of the file.

prompt: What has to be checked before calling two rule sets equivalent?
optionA: That the page looks the same
optionB: That they contain the same number of rules
optionC: That they use the same properties
optionD: That they agree on the markup shown and on markup the selectors might also match
correctAnswerText: That they agree on the markup shown and on markup the selectors might also match
explanation: A stylesheet describes a set of documents rather than one, so agreement on the present markup is only part of the claim. Two rule sets can look identical today and diverge the moment an element is added.
